Commit to one clear answer built around Cornelius instead of a three-part survey that ends in 'Christians still disagree'. Cut the signposting and the Sodom detour.

scripts.name: What if Adam and Eve never ate from the tree?
weakest: Work in that world would feel like tending something you love.
The change at home would be even more striking.
Every prayer you have ever prayed is an attempt to reach across a distance that was never meant to be there.
fixes: Tie every 'what would be different' claim to a specific line from Genesis 2-3 instead of guessing (like the dinner-table and work lines), so the what-if becomes a reveal and not a daydream.

Cut the signpost transitions and anchor each 'what would be different' beat in a surprising textual detail (e.g., the tree of life was never forbidden) instead of speculation like 'work would feel like tending something you love'.
Anchor the speculation in more of the text, such as the tree of life and Genesis 3:22, so each 'what would change' is shown from Scripture and not imagined.

scripts.name: Why didn't God remove the tree?
weakest: So God gave us free will, and He tells us plainly which way to choose.
He knew Adam and Eve would disobey.
So God gave us free will, and He tells us plainly which way to choose.
fixes: Earn the answer from Genesis itself (what the tree's name and the single command reveal) instead of a hypothetical argument built on other commandments.
Replace the hypothetical steal/covet argument with evidence from Genesis itself (what the command, the serpent, or the tree of life reveal) so the free-will answer is earned rather than asserted.
Ground the answer in Genesis itself (what the tree was, the one command, what God said) and cut the hypothetical steal/covet argument, which is asserted rather than shown.

Open on the text's puzzle instead of a sermon to the viewer, e.g. 'Why did God ask Adam where he was if He already knew?', and cut the lines that assume what the viewer has done.
